note: Matched to the GENRE rows that already carry descriptions, which run longer and more taxonomic than the rest of the catalog -- what the genre does, what its discipline is, and where to pair it.

entries.title: Absurdist Comedy
entries.description: Humour drawn from a universe that does not cohere. Rules change without notice, characters respond reasonably to unreasonable conditions, and the joke is the gap between the two.

entries.title: AI Utopia
entries.description: Futures in which artificial minds succeeded at governance and the resulting comfort is genuine. Tension comes from what was traded away for it, not from a machine turning hostile.

entries.title: Alien Invasion
entries.description: First contact conducted as an act of force. Scope runs from a single town to an occupied planet, and the strongest versions care about what the invaded population becomes.

entries.title: Alternate History
entries.description: One documented divergence, followed rigorously. The discipline is in the consequences: what industry, borders and ordinary life look like several decades downstream.

entries.title: Astrobiological Adventure
entries.description: Exploration driven by the search for life rather than territory. Discovery is procedural, the biology is both antagonist and prize, and the crew are specialists rather than soldiers.

entries.title: Crime Noir
entries.description: Crime told from inside the moral compromise. Rain, debt, and a protagonist who solves the case and is not improved by having solved it.

entries.title: Dark Academia
entries.description: Institutions of learning as sites of obsession. Old libraries, closed friendships, a subject pursued well past the point of health, and something the faculty already knew.

entries.title: Dark Fairy Tale
entries.description: Folk structure with the consequences put back. The bargain is real, the woods are not a metaphor, and the ending is earned rather than granted.

entries.title: Dreamlike Surrealism
entries.description: Narrative organised by association rather than causality. Transitions go unexplained and stay internally consistent, and the reader is expected to keep up rather than be caught up.

entries.title: Dystopian Romance
entries.description: Intimacy conducted under a system built to prevent it. The relationship is the act of resistance and the setting supplies the cost.

entries.title: Epic Fantasy
entries.description: Secondary worlds at continental scale, with invented history, multiple cultures, and stakes that reach the shape of the world itself. Long-form by nature.

entries.title: Epistolary Fiction
entries.description: Told entirely through documents: letters, logs, transcripts, recovered messages. The gaps between documents carry as much weight as the documents do.

entries.title: Fantasy Noir
entries.description: Investigation in a world where magic works. The magic never solves the case; it supplies people with new ways to lie.

entries.title: Gaslamp Fantasy
entries.description: A nineteenth-century industrial setting with the supernatural treated as an open fact. Gas light, calling cards, and societies that convene after dark.

entries.title: Grimdark Fantasy
entries.description: Fantasy with the reassurance stripped out. Institutions act in self-interest, violence leaves damage that persists, and heroism is expensive and rarely rewarded.

entries.title: Heroic Fantasy
entries.description: Individual champions against defined threats, at a scale one person can carry. Older and tighter than epic fantasy, and more interested in a single sword than a map.

entries.title: Historical Fantasy
entries.description: A real researched period with the supernatural present and integrated. The history constrains the magic rather than merely decorating it.

entries.title: Horror Fantasy
entries.description: Invented worlds where the fantastic is a source of dread rather than wonder. The rules exist and are learnable, and learning them too late is the plot.

entries.title: Indigenous Futurism
entries.description: Futures authored from Indigenous perspectives, with continuity, sovereignty and land at the centre. Pair with the specific nation or tradition whenever the source is known.

entries.title: Interactive Fiction
entries.description: Narrative in which the reader's choices determine what happens next. Structure is branching or state-driven, and rereading is part of the form rather than a failure of it.

entries.title: Latin American Magical Realism
entries.description: Realist narrative in which the impossible is reported plainly and nobody in the story finds it remarkable. Rooted in specific regional literary traditions rather than a general mood.

entries.title: Lovecraftian Horror
entries.description: Dread built from scale and indifference. Knowledge is the hazard, the antagonist has no interest in humanity, and the protagonist's mind is what stands to be lost.

entries.title: Martian Colonization
entries.description: The particular engineering and politics of settling Mars. Dust, radiation, supply lag, and the question of whose law applies at that distance.

entries.title: Medieval Fantasy
entries.description: The default castle-and-village register, with feudal structure, guilds and a technology ceiling. Familiar enough to build on without stopping to explain.

entries.title: Monster Romance
entries.description: Attraction across the species line, taken seriously by the text. The monstrousness is not resolved by the ending, which is generally the entire point.

entries.title: Musical Adventure
entries.description: Story in which performance drives the plot rather than pausing it. Numbers advance the action and the score belongs to the world.

entries.title: Mystery Sci-Fi
entries.description: An investigation whose solution depends on the speculative element. The technology or biology is the clue, and fair play requires establishing it early.

entries.title: Noir Thriller
entries.description: Pace and paranoia in place of deduction. The protagonist is running, the conspiracy is wider than expected, and the win condition is survival.

entries.title: Nordic Noir
entries.description: Crime in a cold, procedural, socially observant register. Endless light or none at all, institutional detail, and a bleakness that is cultural rather than stylistic.

entries.title: Pirate Adventure
entries.description: Ships, articles, and stolen freedom. The crew is a chosen society with its own written law, and the sea is the only authority that enforces anything.

entries.title: Post-Human Dystopia
entries.description: After the species altered itself. What remains has continuity with humanity and does not share its interests, and the setting is the argument.

entries.title: Psychological Horror
entries.description: The threat is internal, or at least unverifiable. Reliability of perception is the mechanism, and the reader is placed inside the doubt rather than outside it.

entries.title: Retro-Futurism
entries.description: The future as an earlier era pictured it. Fins, valves, atomic optimism, and the particular poignancy of a tomorrow that never showed up.

entries.title: Science Fantasy
entries.description: Both toolkits at once, unapologetically. Starships and sorcery share one world and the text declines to rank them.

entries.title: Science Romance
entries.description: The older name for speculative adventure, from before the genre settled. Extraordinary voyages, scientific wonder, and a nineteenth-century sense of what might be possible.

entries.title: Space Pirates
entries.description: Piracy relocated to the shipping lanes between worlds. Boarding actions, contested salvage, and jurisdictions stretched too thin to enforce anything.

entries.title: Techno-Thriller
entries.description: Near-future tension built on hardware that works as specified. Competence is the pleasure and procedure is the plot.

entries.title: Time Travel
entries.description: Movement through time as the central mechanism, with a stated model of how paradox behaves. That model is the genre's real content.

entries.title: Vampire Gothic
entries.description: The vampire in its inherited setting: old houses, older bloodlines, hunger dressed up as courtesy. Sensual, mannered, and fundamentally about power.

entries.title: Weird Fantasy
entries.description: Invented worlds that refuse the familiar template. Biology, economics and geography are strange on purpose, and the strangeness is load-bearing.

entries.title: Biopunk
entries.description: Genetic engineering as street technology. Bodies modified in back rooms, corporations that own sequences, and consequences carried in the flesh.

entries.title: Dystopia
entries.description: A society organised around one controlling premise, followed to its conclusion. The reader watches the system working exactly as designed, which is the horror.

entries.title: Hopepunk
entries.description: Deliberate resistance to grimdark. Kindness as a repeated political act, cooperation as strategy, and the fight continuing without any guarantee of winning.

entries.title: Isekai
entries.description: A protagonist transported into another world and required to function there. Knowledge from the prior world is the advantage; homesickness is the price.

entries.title: Nanopunk
entries.description: Molecular machines as ambient infrastructure. Everything is programmable at a scale nobody can observe, and trust becomes the scarce resource.

entries.title: Noir
entries.description: The register itself: moral fog, doomed decisions, and a city that shapes the people inside it. Applies well beyond crime.

entries.title: Pastoral
entries.description: Rural life rendered as an ideal, the labour softened and the seasons brought forward. The tension almost always arrives from outside.

entries.title: Shonen
entries.description: Serialized adventure for a young audience, built on escalating challenge, training, rivalry and earned friendship. The structure is the appeal.

entries.title: Thriller
entries.description: Sustained forward pressure with a clock running. Stakes are personal and immediate, and the reader is kept deliberately ahead of or behind the protagonist.

entries.title: Western
entries.description: Frontier as moral setting: thin law, contested land, and violence as the instrument at hand. The genre is about what settlement costs.
